title: 124 Breeds, breeding practices, and health management of sheep flocks in Arkansas, USA
content:
Abstract
The sheep industry is growing in Arkansas. The inventory has increased by 9% annually in the last five years. However, information about production systems is scarce. An online survey was conducted in October 2023 to obtain information about breeds, breeding practices, and health management. Seventy-seven producers from 39 counties (out of 75) responded to the survey. Katahdin (62%), crossbred sheep (47%), and Dorper (39%) were the most common breeds. The main criteria for selection were health (93%), reproduction (90%), maternal traits (75%), appearance (70%), and growth/weight gain (65%). Most farmers (74%) adopted the culling rate from 1% to 10%. Nearly all producers (94%) used natural mating for breeding their flock (average ram:ewe ratio of 1:16). However, 15% used artificial insemination and 7% embryo transfer, using CIDR to administer progesterone and half of those (56%) also administered prostaglandin or GnRH while 44% used both. The lambing rate was satisfactory, with 55% of producers indicating more than 120 lambs per 100 ewes (18%, >160; 21%, 140-160 and 16%, 120-140). However, about 18% of farmers were unsure of their lambing rate, which indicated a need for education since it is a key indicator of productivity. Lamb mortality rate was low, with 61% and 20% of producers reporting less than 5% and 6-10%, respectively. Internal parasites were the primary health issue (75% of respondents), followed by foot rot/foot scald (55%). Vaccinations were performed only by 70% of farmers, which shows a need for more emphasis in future producer education programs. Drenching and hoof care were the most common husbandry practices (83 and 86%, respectively), and generally producers deworm animals and trim hooves only when needed (61 and 70%, respectively). Moxidectin, levamisole, albendazole, ivermectin, and fenbendazole were the most widely used anthelmintics, as indicated by 74%, 66%, 51%, 45%, and 34% of farmers, respectively. Copper oxide wire particles (COWP) were not commonly used (36%) to manage internal parasites, even though previous work has shown that Haemonchus contortus is the main parasite in Arkansas, and COWP is an effective tool to control it. When an animal gets sick, producers most commonly check the eyes (97%), check for dehydration (63%), and take rectal temperatures (54%). In conclusion, extension personnel should focus on providing resources and education to producers on record keeping, animal selection, vaccination, internal parasite management, and hoof health.
